title: A Mumbai Textile Mill and a Himalayan 16-Seater Just Rewrote India's Fine Dining Story
excerpt: Masque won Asia's Art of Hospitality Award and NAAR leapt 36 places to No. 30 — together, they represent India's strongest showing ever at Asia's 50 Best Restaurants.
body:
On the evening of March 25 at the Kerry Hotel in Hong Kong, while The Chairman reclaimed the top spot on Asia's 50 Best Restaurants list, two Indian restaurants quietly made history.

Masque, the decade-old tasting menu institution inside a repurposed textile mill in Mumbai's Mahalaxmi district, rose to No. 15 and became the first Indian restaurant ever to receive the Art of Hospitality Award. NAAR, a 16-seat restaurant perched above the Himalayan treeline near Kasauli, jumped from No. 66 to No. 30 in a single year. One is the product of ten years of accumulated conviction. The other is barely two years old. Neither is in a city that usually gets this kind of attention.

## Masque: hospitality as an ecosystem

Founded in 2016 by entrepreneur Aditi Dugar, Masque has earned its reputation through immersive ten-course tasting menus that spotlight seasonal, locally sourced, and foraged ingredients from across India — from Kashmir's forests to Goa's coastline. Head chef Varun Totlani, a Culinary Institute of America graduate named Condé Nast Traveller's Chef of the Year in 2025, leads a kitchen that treats regional Indian produce with the technical ambition usually reserved for Scandinavian or Japanese gastronomy.

The Art of Hospitality Award, voted on by more than 350 members of the Asia's 50 Best Academy, recognised Masque not just for impeccable service but for building, in the Academy's words, "a complete ecosystem of hospitality around modern Indian gastronomy." Responding to the win, Dugar described the recognition as a milestone in Masque's tenth year: "It reaffirms what we've been trying to achieve since Masque opened its doors — to treat every guest with care, generosity, and humility."

The restaurant has since taken that ecosystem on the road. From June 4 to 8, Masque staged a culinary residency at Bangkok's Siam Kempinski Hotel — an eight-course experience at THB 4,950 per person that brought Mumbai's ingredient-driven storytelling to Thailand's dining capital.

## NAAR: the Himalayan wildcard

NAAR's ascent is arguably more dramatic. Tucked into the hills above Kasauli in Himachal Pradesh, it seats just 16 guests and serves a menu rooted in Himalayan terroir — wild herbs, mountain mushrooms, locally milled grains. Its leap of 36 places in a single year is among the largest on the 2026 list and suggests that the global fine dining establishment is paying real attention to what's happening beyond India's metros.

## What this means for NRI food lovers

For diaspora Indians who grew up hearing that "real" Indian food could only be found in home kitchens, Masque and NAAR represent something new: Indian restaurants that compete at the highest levels of global gastronomy without abandoning the flavours, ingredients, or storytelling that make the cuisine what it is. They are not chasing Western validation by cooking French technique with Indian spices. They are cooking Indian food, full stop, and the world is coming to them.

The next time you plan a trip home, skip the usual itinerary. Book a seat at a textile mill in Mumbai or a 16-seater in the Himalayas. The waiting list may be the hardest part.

*Sources: Asia's 50 Best Restaurants, Kempinski Hotels, Robb Report India, Remote Lands, The Dot Magazine*
